passage: Jasleen watched the gate of the nursery each morning while waiting for her own bus. Rajni, about two, arrived with her father and cried. One day her father slipped away while she looked at a toy; when she turned, she screamed. The next day he did the same steps: a kiss, a wave, and "back after snack." Rajni cried, then waved through the window, cried a bit again, and finally walked to the sand tray. Jasleen could not tell what Rajni felt inside.

qa.q: What three things did Rajni's father do at goodbye on the second day?
qa.a: He gave her a kiss, waved, and told her he would be back after snack.

qa.q: What might Rajni have felt when she turned and her father was gone, and what other explanation is there for her scream?
qa.a: She probably felt startled and abandoned because he vanished without warning. She could also simply have been overtired that morning.

qa.q: What could the father keep doing to help Rajni at drop-off?
qa.a: He can keep the same short, predictable goodbye every day and always say goodbye rather than slipping out. 🙂

qa.q: How does Jasleen understand what she sees?
qa.a: She sees the crying and waving and the calmer walk to the sand tray, but she is honest that she cannot know Rajni's inner feelings.

grounding: A toddler at drop-off cries and waves in turns, and a predictable farewell ritual helps more than sneaking away.

passage: Day one, Neelam waited until Swati was busy with a puzzle and tiptoed out of the daycare room. Swati looked up, saw the empty door and wailed for a long time. Day four, Neelam knelt down: "One hug, one wave, then I go. I come back after your nap." Swati clung, then waved. Day ten, she hugged, sobbed briefly at the window, waved, and walked to the toy kitchen, wiping her cheeks.

qa.q: What words did Neelam use in the goodbye routine on day four?
qa.a: She said, "One hug, one wave, then I go. I come back after your nap."

qa.q: What was Swati likely feeling on day one when she saw the empty door, and what else could have added to it?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and confused because her mother disappeared without a word. She may also have already been tired or unsettled.

qa.q: What made the later goodbyes easier?
qa.a: The same short ritual every day let Swati know what would happen and when Neelam would return.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel while walking away on day ten?
qa.a: She may feel a pang seeing Swati's tears but also relief and trust that the routine is helping.

grounding: A short predictable farewell ritual regulates a toddler's mixed goodbye feelings better than sneaking away.

passage:
For weeks, Shankar had slipped out of the Chennai daycare while Jaya was busy, and every day she searched the room, sobbing. This week he tried something new: two hugs, one high-five, and a wave at the window.
Today Jaya clung to his neck and cried. Then she took the high-five. Then she cried again. But she went to the window and waved, tears on her cheeks, and turned back to the blocks.

qa.q: What was the new goodbye Shankar tried?
qa.a: Two hugs, one high-five and a wave at the window.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling at drop-off today?
qa.a: She was sad about the goodbye, clinging and crying, but also able to wave and turn to the blocks, showing mixed feelings she could manage.

qa.q: Why does the ritual work better than slipping out?
qa.a: Because Jaya knows what will happen and when he leaves, so she doesn't have to search the room in fear.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel walking away after the wave?
qa.a: He probably feels a pang at her tears, but also relief that she turned back to play.

grounding: A father replaces sneaking away with a short goodbye ritual, which helps his toddler manage mixed feelings at drop-off.

passage:
"Just slip out while he's playing, Imran," said Ujjwal's mother. "He won't notice."
"Last time he noticed. He searched every room and screamed for an hour."
"So what, then?"
"Our goodbye." Imran knelt. "Ujjwal. Bye-bye kiss. Papa comes after nap."
Ujjwal's lip wobbled. He cried and held on. Imran kissed him, said it once more and stood. Ujjwal cried, then lifted a hand and waved.

qa.q: When did Imran say he would come back?
qa.a: After nap.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling at the goodbye?
qa.a: He was sad and upset, crying and holding on, but able to wave, showing mixed feelings that the ritual helped him manage.

qa.q: Why did Imran choose the goodbye over slipping out?
qa.a: Because slipping out last time left Ujjwal searching and screaming, while a clear, short goodbye tells him what is happening.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's mother see the goodbye at first?
qa.a: She thinks slipping out would be easier and that he wouldn't notice.

grounding: A father uses a short, predictable goodbye rather than sneaking away, helping his toddler cope with a sad drop-off.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. Until last week, Kishore's mother left while he was distracted, and he would cry at the door for a long time. This week we agreed on a ritual: one song, one hug, and a wave from the window. Today he cried during the song, hugged her tight, and then ran to the window to wave. He sniffed for a few minutes and then joined the sand tray. Much quicker than before. Preeti, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Kishore join after sniffing?
qa.a: The sand tray.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling during the new goodbye?
qa.a: He was still sad, crying during the song and hugging tight, but the familiar steps helped him feel safe enough to wave and settle quickly.

qa.q: What would you advise other parents at this daycare?
qa.a: Use a short, predictable goodbye ritual instead of leaving while the child is distracted.

qa.q: How might Kishore's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and encouraged that he settled much quicker.

grounding: A teacher records how a short, predictable goodbye ritual helped a toddler settle faster than sneaking away.

passage:
Outside the anganwadi in the kasba, Saurabh clung to his Maa's sari.
She knelt. “Two kisses. One wave at the window. After khichdi, Maa comes.” Kiss, kiss.
Saurabh cried and held on. Then he let Farhan, the helper, lift him. He waved. Then cried again.
Last month she used to slip away while he played, and he screamed for an hour.
Now, at the window, Saurabh waved once more. His crying slowed to hiccups.

qa.q: When does Maa say she will come back?
qa.a: After khichdi, Maa comes.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he cried, clung and waved in turns?
qa.a: He was sad and anxious about Maa leaving, while also starting to accept the goodbye, so his feelings were mixed.

qa.q: Why does the short goodbye routine work better than slipping away?
qa.a: It is predictable and tells Saurabh what will happen, so he can manage his distress; sneaking away left him screaming for an hour.

qa.q: How might Maa feel doing the goodbye while Saurabh cries?
qa.a: She probably feels sad and torn, but reassured when his crying slows at the window.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler at drop-off crying, clinging and waving in turns, and a short predictable farewell ritual helping more than sneaking away.
